attacks.claim: The 'rename' is actually ADD COLUMN then DROP COLUMN with no data copy. On deploy, every user's notes (user-written, unrecoverable elsewhere) are permanently destroyed across ~140M rows. The down migration likewise adds an empty notes column and drops private_notes, so rollback cannot restore data either.
attacks.evidence:
ALTER TABLE user_recipes ADD COLUMN private_notes text;
ALTER TABLE user_recipes DROP COLUMN notes;  /  PR text: 'Pure rename, no data change; the down migration restores the old name.'

attacks.claim: The PR description claims a pure rename, but the SQL is a destructive swap. The description contradicts the code, and reviewers or operators relying on it will not expect data loss. ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN was the correct, instant, metadata-only operation.
attacks.evidence: 'Pure rename, no data change' vs. ADD COLUMN + DROP COLUMN in 0087_private_notes.up.sql

attacks.claim: Migrations run automatically on deploy, and the old code still reads `notes` while the new code reads `private_notes`. During rolling deploy, old instances will hit 'column notes does not exist' errors, since the rename is not backward-compatible (no expand/contract). There is also no backup or guard before auto-running.
attacks.evidence: 'Migrations run automatically on deploy after merge to main.' Old query: `ur.notes` vs. new `ur.private_notes`

attacks.claim: The cursor pagination fetches ALL of a user's saved recipes (200k+ for heavy users, with join and sort) on every request, then slices in memory. It is O(N) per page, so paging through is O(N²/limit). Memory and latency blow the 300ms p99 budget and create a DoS vector. This is worse than the original LIMIT/OFFSET query.
attacks.evidence: ORDER BY ur.saved_at DESC, ur.id DESC`, [userId]);  const start = ... rows.findIndex(...) ; rows.slice(start, start + limit)

attacks.claim: The cursor is the row id located via findIndex. If the cursor row was deleted or is invalid, findIndex returns -1, so start becomes 0 and the client silently restarts from page one, possibly looping forever. Also, an empty result with a limit set gives page[page.length-1] on an empty array only if start+limit<rows.length, which is unlikely but unguarded. A keyset cursor (saved_at,id) in SQL would be stable.
attacks.evidence: const start = cursor ? rows.findIndex((r) => r.id === cursor) + 1 : 0;

attacks.claim: The existing offset parameter is dropped with no compatibility handling. Tests only cover the happy path, with no tests for an invalid or deleted cursor, the migration, or data preservation.
attacks.evidence: Test only 'pages with cursor' happy path; no migration test

attacks.claim: Two unrelated changes (a destructive schema change and a pagination rewrite) are bundled in one PR, which makes review and rollback harder.
attacks.evidence: 'Two small changes bundled because they touch the same table.'
